analysis.one_liner: Diverts part of Social Security payroll taxes into personal investment accounts while cutting guaranteed benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: referred to the Ways and Means subcommittee on Social Security in March 2004, it never received a hearing or vote before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have redirected roughly a third of the employee share of the Social Security payroll tax into an individual investment account for everyone born after 1949, run by the government on a federal-employee-retirement model, with the option to move the money to a private investment firm once the balance passed $7,500. To pay for it, the bill trimmed the guaranteed benefit in many ways: a new inflation measure that would slow cost-of-living increases, a rewritten benefit formula, steeper penalties for retiring early, and a faster rise in the retirement age. It also added a minimum benefit floor for long-career low earners, raised widows' benefits, and let low-income workers put part of their earned income tax credit into their account with a federal match.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers born after 1949 would own an individual account funded by their own payroll deductions, investable in federal fund options or, above a $7,500 balance, with a private investment firm; balances pass to heirs at death. Low-wage workers with long careers would get a higher minimum monthly benefit, widows and widowers would get larger benefits, and Earned Income Tax Credit recipients could route part of their refund into the account with a 50% federal match. Investment firms, insurers, and credit unions certified by the SEC would gain a new market managing these accounts, and annuity providers would gain mandatory purchases of lifetime income at retirement.

how_it_helps.text: Every worker born after 1949 would get an individual account funded by an employee payroll deduction of 3% on the first $10,000 of wages and 2% above that, with the option to contribute up to $5,000 more, held in a federally administered fund modeled on the federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan.

Once an account balance reaches $7,500, the holder could shift the entire account to a private investment firm, credit union, or insurance company certified by the SEC; account balances are inherited by the holder's heirs if the holder dies before retiring.
The bill creates a minimum monthly Social Security benefit based on quarters worked, phasing in from 2010, and increases widow's and widower's benefits.

Earned Income Tax Credit recipients could designate part of their credit as a contribution to their account and receive a federal match of 50% of designated wages, self-employment income, and EITC amounts, up to $600 per year plus $150.

analysis.who_pays: Future retirees and disability beneficiaries would pay through a smaller guaranteed benefit: cost-of-living adjustments would be cut by a new 'CPI overstatement' measure applied to Social Security and most other federal benefit programs, the benefit formula would be rewritten to pay less to middle and higher earners, early retirement would be penalized more steeply, and the rise in the eligibility age would accelerate. General taxpayers would pay through new transfers from the general fund to the Social Security trust fund to cover the money diverted into accounts, and account holders would bear all investment losses with no government guarantee.

drawbacks.text: The bill finances the accounts by cutting the guaranteed benefit: it subtracts a published 'CPI overstatement' from the inflation measure used for Social Security cost-of-living adjustments and for retiree, disability, and other federal benefits, and phases in lower benefit-formula percentages for everyone becoming eligible after 2005.

Account holders sign an acknowledgment that investments are made at their own risk and are not protected by the government or the trustee against loss, and trustees are shielded from liability for losses unless they acted unreasonably by clear and convincing evidence.
The bill accelerates the increase in the Social Security eligibility age and steepens the actuarial penalty for retiring early, taking effect for people becoming eligible after 2003.

It caps the combined benefit of a married couple at the level of the maximum worker benefit, and cuts the share of Social Security revenue transferred to the Medicare trust fund by 10 percentage points per year after 2010.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a real gain — personal accounts workers own and can pass on, a minimum benefit for low earners, and matched contributions for EITC recipients — against a broad set of cuts to the guaranteed benefit that every current and future beneficiary would feel, especially through the slower inflation index. The accounts themselves carry no guarantee: a worker who retired into a downturn would bear the loss. It is a genuine trade-off rather than a free lunch, and the question of whether market returns and ownership justify smaller guaranteed checks was never tested, because the bill never got a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, passed to the Social Security subcommittee two weeks later, and sat there until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005 with no hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Kolbe introduced the bill with Rep. Charles Stenholm on February 24, 2004; the House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and, for relevant provisions, the Rules Committee the same day.
On March 10, 2004, it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security; the action history records no hearing, markup, or vote after that referral.
The bill had a single cosponsor, a Democrat, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, so the bill expired without reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The traditional Social Security benefit formula, retirement ages, and inflation index were left untouched, so current and future beneficiaries kept the existing guaranteed benefit. The investment industry did not gain the new account-management market the bill would have created.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Social Security on March 10, 2004, and took no further action on it; no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the action history.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican and a conservative Democrat introduced the bill together, but with only one cosponsor and no vote ever taken, no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Investment and financial services firms (mutual funds, brokerages, credit unions)
industries.note: The bill would make certified private institutions the permanent managers of a stream of mandatory payroll deductions, with account holders allowed to move their full balance to a private firm once it reaches $7,500. Management fees would come out of workers' retirement savings, and holders waive protection against investment losses.

Insurers could be certified as account custodians, and retirees would be required to use part of their account balance to buy annuities or lifetime monthly payments, creating a large captive annuity market.

The bill rewrites payroll withholding to split the employee contribution between the trust fund and individual accounts and directs regulators to design designation rules to avoid undue burdens on employers, who would still face new administrative work.
